messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Fawn Response: become overly compliant when feeling threatened
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The night the storm came, Chidera was in the operating room. She was a third-year surgical resident, the youngest on her team, and she had been assisting in a complex bowel resection when the hospital’s backup generator failed. The lights flickered, held, then died completely. For twelve minutes, she stood in total darkness, the patient open on the table, the wind howling against the windows like something alive. She could hear the gurneys rolling in the hall, the crash of debris against the glass, and the attending surgeon’s voice, steady and calm, telling everyone to stay where they were. When the lights came back, she saw the patient’s vitals had dipped dangerously low. They stabilized him, finished the surgery, and she went home at dawn to find her apartment building had lost its roof. For weeks afterward, she told herself she was fine. She had to be fine. She was a surgeon.

But the fine began to crack. Now, four months later, Chidera cannot hear the rumble of a passing truck without her chest seizing. A sudden clatter of metal instruments in the OR makes her jump so badly she nearly drops a clamp. She has started to dread the night shift, not because of the work, but because of the darkness that settles over the hospital after midnight. When she wakes in the dark of her own bedroom, her heart is already pounding before her mind catches up, and she lies still, listening to the silence, certain that something is about to go wrong. The weather forecasts have become a source of dread; any mention of thunderstorms sends a spike of cold fear through her, and she finds herself checking the radar on her phone obsessively, even on clear days. These moments of alarm, the sudden startle and the racing pulse, have come to feel like proof that she is still in danger. She has come to believe that her body is telling her the truth: the world is not safe, and she cannot trust herself to stay calm.

Because she cannot trust herself, Chidera has begun to control everything she can. She forces herself to breathe slowly and evenly during surgeries, clenching her jaw against the urge to flinch. She has stopped running, her only outlet, because the rhythm of her own footsteps and the sound of her own breath remind her too much of that panicked, gasping moment in the dark. She has become overly agreeable with her attending surgeons, nodding and smiling even when she disagrees, terrified that any sign of resistance will mark her as unreliable. She tries to keep her emotions locked down, but the effort exhausts her, and the exhaustion makes her feel even more fragile. The harder she works to control herself, the more convinced she becomes that she is one small trigger away from falling apart. She is certain that her life has been destroyed, that she can no longer rely on her own instincts, and that no matter what she does, bad things will keep happening.

The cycle tightens. Every time she startles at a sound, she interprets it as proof that she is broken. Every time she avoids exercise or suppresses a feeling, she feels a little more helpless. She has begun to scan the faces of her colleagues for signs that they have noticed her jumpiness, and the hypervigilance only makes her more reactive. She finds herself avoiding the trauma bay where the patient from that night was stabilized, taking the long way around the hospital to her office. She has started coming in early to check the weather report before every shift, and on days when rain is predicted, she calls in sick, inventing a headache or a stomach bug. She knows this is not sustainable. Her performance reviews have slipped. She was once the rising star of her residency; now she is the one who looks tired and distracted.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment in the OR last week. A scrub nurse dropped a scalpel, and the sound of it hitting the tile floor sent Chidera into a full-body flinch. The attending surgeon looked at her, not unkindly, and said, “You okay, Chidera?” She had smiled and nodded, but that night she could not sleep. She lay in the dark, replaying the sound of the scalpel, the look on the surgeon’s face, and she realized she was afraid of what would happen if she did not get help. She is most afraid that she will lose her career, the one thing she has worked for her entire life. But underneath that, she is afraid that she has already lost herself—that the person who walked into the OR that night, confident and steady, is gone. She is hoping that talking to someone will help her find a way back.
